Holpen
HOL-pen
v. (archaic past participle of help)
Archaic past participle of help; Old English holpen (helped, aided), past participle of helpan. Renders the Greek antilambanō, “to take hold of, help, support,” in Luke 1:54.

📖 Biblical Definition

Holpen is the archaic past participle of help—an Old English form that the KJV preserves in one of its most celebrated passages, the Magnificat: he hath holpen his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy (Luke 1:54). Modern English long ago shifted the past participle to helped; the KJV retains the older form, which carries a distinctive cadence and an antique dignity. The Greek behind it—antilambanō—means literally to take hold of in turn, to take hold against, and pictures God reaching out to take hold of His servant Israel against the weight of her need and her enemies. The verb’s biblical pattern, broader than this single archaic-English form, traces God’s sustained help of His people across redemptive history. He holpen His servant Israel in remembrance of His mercy, the Magnificat says; He holpen them out of Egypt by the hand of Moses; He holpen them through the wilderness with manna and water; He holpen them in the conquest by the sword of the angel of the LORD; He holpen them in the days of the judges by the deliverers He raised up; He holpen them by the hand of David against the Philistines and the surrounding kingdoms; He holpen them through the captivity by the providences that preserved a remnant; and supremely He has holpen them in the sending of the Saviour, the Son of Mary, the seed of Abraham, the Son of David, the One whose advent the Magnificat itself celebrates. Holpen as a word therefore carries a long memory: the long history of God’s help to His people, against which the present help (Christ’s incarnation) is the consummate instance. The KJV’s retention of the antique form is fitting; the antique form carries the antique memory.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines HOLPEN as the past participle of help (archaic), as in the Magnificat: he hath holpen his servant Israel (Luke 1:54).

expand to see more

HOLPEN, ppr. or pp. — Archaic past participle of help; helped. He hath holpen his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy (Luke 1:54). The modern past participle is helped, but the archaic form is preserved in the KJV.

HELP, v.t. — To aid; to assist; to lend strength or means towards effecting a purpose; as, to help a man in his work.

📖 Key Scripture

Luke 1:54-55 — "He hath holpen his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy; As he spake to our fathers, to Abraham, and to his seed for ever."

Acts 26:22 — "Having therefore obtained help of God, I continue unto this day, witnessing both to small and great..."

Hebrews 4:16 — "Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need."

Psalm 121:1-2 — "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help. My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Holpen is corrupted (by the standards of modern accessibility) by retaining the archaic form most readers no longer recognize—but the loss of the form, in modern translations, is also the loss of the cadence and dignity by which the Magnificat’s long memory of God’s help across the generations is rhetorically carried.

expand to see more

Modern translations uniformly replace holpen with the contemporary helped, on grounds of accessibility. The trade is real. Helped is immediately understood; holpen requires explanation. But what is lost in the modernization is not merely a vocabulary item but a register: the antique form carries the antique memory, the Magnificat’s long backward look across the centuries of God’s help to Israel is borne by the language that itself comes from centuries past. He hath holpen his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy, as he spake to our fathers, to Abraham, and to his seed for ever—the cadence of the verse is doing work that the flatter modern he has helped his servant Israel, remembering to be merciful cannot replicate. The KJV reader who learns the antique form recovers access to the cadence and dignity by which Mary’s song reaches back across the generations of Israel’s covenant history.

This is the general pastoral case for the KJV’s antique vocabulary, of which holpen is one specimen. The archaic forms are not preserved as obstacles to comprehension but as bearers of a rhetorical register modern English has largely lost. The reader who acquires the small skill of reading them recovers access not only to the meanings but to the depth of address Scripture in its English tradition has been given. The case is not against modern translations as such (which have their proper uses) but against the assumption that modernization is sheer gain. Holpen is a small case that illustrates the larger pattern: the KJV is not merely accurate; it is rhetorically formed in a register that has shaped English Christian piety for four centuries, and the saint who reads it in its own idiom hears Scripture in a register the modernization has, sometimes, quietly lost.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English holpen, past participle of helpan (to help); renders Greek antilambanō (to take hold of, help, support—Luke 1:54); preserved in the KJV in the Magnificat’s celebrated retrospection of God’s help to His servant Israel across the generations.

expand to see more

Old English holpen — archaic past participle of helpan, to help.

Greek antilambanō (G482) — to take hold of, help, support (Luke 1:54; Acts 20:35; 1 Tim 6:2).

Hebrew ‘āzar (H5826) — to help, aid (the great OT help-verb).

Hebrew ‘ezer (H5828) — help, aid (Gen 2:18, the woman as a help meet for man).

Usage

"He hath holpen his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy—the Magnificat’s long backward look across the centuries of God’s help."

"Holpen retains the antique cadence by which Mary’s song reaches across the generations; the modern helped flattens the register."

"The case for the KJV’s antique vocabulary is not against modernization as such but for the recognition that the older forms carry a rhetorical register the modern equivalents have, sometimes, lost."
